title: Comala's Callers
subtitle: For a drifter, a stay behind an iron-barred window can feel like just another stretch of desert.

trails.title: The Weaving of Shadows, Volume I
trails.description: Darkness has no form. The ever-shifting gaze seeps into every crevice.

trails.title: To the Pen Pal I Never Met
trails.description: Perhaps the pen pal you never see is the one you truly need.

content.text: To the Pen Pal I Never Met

Aleph, my dear pen pal, enclosed is the latest revision of my novel. In your last letter, you suggested the role of a bank clerk, marking Amalfitano with the stamp of the capitalist production model—an excellent idea! In this revision, I have incorporated some of my own thoughts as well.

...

That is everything about my novel that I was impatient to share with you. Perhaps you won't mind me discussing something else? Throughout my creative journey, your encouragement and validation have been my greatest comfort when facing the countless closed doors of publishers. The long, futile efforts feel insignificant in the face of your understanding. Oh, my dear pen pal, I say this sincerely—though I suppose such explanations are unnecessary. Perhaps I do not need to waste more ink describing just how much your letters mean to me. So, I ask, with both sincerity and trepidation: may we speak in person—about the dead, the desert, fate, the ending that troubles me so much, and the tides of imagination and insight that carry us both?

Recoleta,

At the poetry gathering in Santafé de Bogotá's open-air theater, Colombia


Miss Recoleta, as I have mentioned several times in my letters—and as you may have already surmised—I reside in a prison. This is why I have never met my pen pals in person. Due to its remote location and cold climate, Ushuaia is not a place people readily visit. People would rather sip a hot drink in one of Buenos Aires's century-old cafés than travel such a distance.

...

Finally, I still wish you the best on your creative path.

Aleph,

At the Comala Prison in Ushuaia

items.text: Comala's Callers
Day after day, the Paracausality Researcher hid away in the wilderness outside the town of Amalfitano studying the data she had collected.
One evening at dusk, a voice called out from outside her cave. She put down the equipment and her tapes and stepped outside. A man stood curiously at her door.
"What are you doing here?" he asked, raising both eyebrows. "Nothing ever happens in Amalfitano these days."
The local introduced himself as the Bank Clerk. He had probably the most amiable face around—bright eyes, lifted cheeks, a soft jawline. It was a face beaming with hope.
The Researcher showed him the spectrums she'd been compiling. "I've been collecting stories about the Die," she explained. "Perhaps they hold the key to explaining the randomness that fate displays."
"Ah, that does intrigue me so!" the Bank Clerk replied briskly, "I'd love to hear all about it. But I have to go. I mustn't be late to the Dune Piscator's funeral." And with that, he left.
Three days later, the same footsteps returned to her cave.
"You're back! How have you been? Did you make it to the funeral?" She asked.

"I have no idea what you're talking about," he replied tersely. "I'm not the man you think I am." His face was drained and gaunt, his eyes sunken deep into hollow sockets. It was as if every spark of life had been drawn out of him, leaving only an empty husk.
The Researcher insisted she wasn't mistaken. "I know people by their deeper nature, down to the synchronicity of their spectrums. I've never been wrong before."

"Whatever you say." The man muttered roughly. "I don't understand anything of your high-minded ideas. Just let me go. It's been a long day out there fishing, and all I want now is to collapse on my rickety bed." He trudged off with footsteps that sounded exactly like those of the Bank Clerk's.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: As you might have noticed, Ms. Vertin, this facility isn't just a prison. It's also a research center.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: Its full name is "the Panopticon of Comala." It was established by the Foucault Association in 1975.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: We've hosted workshops, academic sessions, and even lectures about the Panopticon. You may even have seen some reports about it.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: Experts of psychoanalysis and scholars from various fields have come here to exchange ideas and seek collaboration in their studies.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: In many ways, the Panopticon is unlike any other prison you've seen before.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: I see. No wonder Ms. Recoleta has gone to such lengths to become a part of it.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Actually, my assistant and I are here to inquire about a prisoner named Dores. Does that name sound familiar?
Corridor, Comala Prison

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: Not that I recall. Could she have used a different name? What does she look like?

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Hmm. She'd have arrived here about three days ago. It's also possible that she came as a visitor, not a prisoner.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: She's a blind woman who always carries an old typewriter.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: She used to be a doctor at the São Paulo Veterans' Residence in Brazil.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: And on the subject of different names, she once wrote for UTTU under the name "Urd."

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: I don't think I've seen anyone fitting that description. And as I said, we haven't had any visitors in some time. Certainly not in the last three days.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: But I did see her! I saw her walking towards Comala Prison!

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: Someone must have mixed up their memories. Simply put, I don't recall seeing anyone by that name or with that description here.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: I see. Thank you, Miss. Perhaps we made a mistake.
Sensing that her current line of questioning is going nowhere, she shifts toward a different topic.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Ms. Recoleta, you've gone to great lengths to get into the Panopticon. Would you mind telling us why?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Finally! I've been waiting for you to ask!

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: I'm here to find my pen pal in Comala!

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: You have a pen pal ... in here?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Yes. Six months ago, I went to a book exhibition in Guadalajara and came across the contact details of a few writers. I sent them my novel and asked for feedback.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Looking back, it was a bit forward. But nothing unheard of between writers. A lot of friendships start through letters, you see.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: And Aleph wrote back.
Recoleta produces a thick stack of letters from her coat.
The recipient's address changes with each letter, reflecting the turbulent lifestyle of the wandering writer, yet the sender's address is eternally constant—Comala.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: And how much do you know about this pen pal of yours?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Oh, well. He calls himself "Aleph," which is a grammatically masculine word, so—

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: So you assume Aleph is a man.
A reasonable suspicion, but in her experience, never a certainty.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Yes. He's probably a poet, a writer, perhaps even an alchemist. He's one of the brightest people I know. There's never been a question that he couldn't answer!

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: I've asked him about religion, politics, history, potions, even critters in length and breadth. Can you imagine someone who knows all those things and so extensively too?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: And he helped me with my novel. He always seems to know the best ways to bring my characters to life.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Honestly, he's so insightful. I've begun wondering if he's omniscient.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: With his help, my story grew richer and fuller, like a well-tended plant. Strangely, I can't seem to take it any further now. It's as if the roots have been sapped of their strength.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: I couldn't understand why. So, I resolved that I would see him in person to find out.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: Again with this story about your uncanny pen pal. I've already told you a dozen times.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: It's all very moving, but it still doesn't justify your actions.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: Writers experience mental blocks all the time. Yet you don't see them trying to break into a prison over it.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: She does have a point.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Please, Vertin, Jailer! Have a little mercy, will you?

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Hold on. I've been meaning to ask—why are you only calling her "Jailer"?

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Don't you know her name? Or do you just prefer addressing people by their occupation?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Oh, about that—
Unexpectedly, it is the jaguar herself that speaks up.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: It's okay, Ms. Vertin. I don't mind being called by my job title. I take pride in what I do.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: I'm perfectly fine with just being "the jailer."

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Exactly! A researcher is a researcher, and a jailer is a jailer.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Titles and code names often tell us more about people than their ordinary given names, don't you think? Take Sonetto, for example.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Your name comes from sonnets, doesn't it? That great poetic form from Italy.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Some people mistakenly think Shakespeare invented it; some say it was Petrarca ... Though no one really knows when the first sonnet was written.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Sorry, I'm straying from my point. You're Italian, aren't you, Sonetto? Is that your real name, or just a code name? Were your parents poets?

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Umm. As much as I'd like to be able to answer your question, I never knew my parents.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: My earliest memories were of the School of Primary Defense of Mankind. I've lived there since I was a small child.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Ah. My apologies. That was thoughtless of me.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: It's fine. You meant no ill intent, I'm sure.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Timekeeper, if Ms. Recoleta was right about Dr. Dores's whereabouts, perhaps the jailer is keeping things from us, or perhaps Dr. Dores visited the Panopticon without her knowledge. Either way, we need to do some digging here.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: I agree. Let's see if we can talk to some of the inmates and find out what they know.
As they chat, the corridors—until now endless—reach a terminal point, with voices echoing ahead.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: Ladies, we're about to enter the main hall of the Panopticon.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: This is one of the places where the inmates spend their recreation time. At this hour, they're supposed to be in their cells. But what's all that noise?
The jailer seems to be tense with the apparently unusual amount of noise.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: Ms. Vertin, could you keep an eye on Recoleta if anything happens?
Recoleta tries her best to avoid the hard stare of the feline jailer by blending into the Foundation team.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Certainly.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: What do you take me for? I'm not going to run away!

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: That'd be a pretty cheesy way to start a story!

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: Please just stay close to me.
